The prices continue to hit voters' pocketbooks.
AAA says the national average for gallon of regular gasoline is $4.17 and for diesel,
it's about $6.30.
The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to weigh in on a dispute
over 20,000 ballots in California.
And PR's Kerry Johnson reports the request comes one day before the midterms.
The Justice Department is making the emergency push in an effort to set aside tens of thousands
of ballots in California that DOJ says could involve non-citizens who unlawfully cast votes.
The administration says those ballots should not be counted until voters' citizenship
status can be affirmed.
Lower courts have sided with California, which maintains its voter rolls are reliable.
Those judges say they're trying to avoid chaos and disenfranchising voters on the eve of elections.
The Supreme Court recently rebuffed a separate effort by President Trump
to restrict mail-in ballots this year.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
A federal judge is throwing out a criminal complaint against two former FBI officials
accused of lying to Congress about former President Joe Biden's son, Hunter.
The judge says the investigation had critical mistakes and was overtly political.
The Justice Department could still appeal or pursue an indictment from a grand jury.
Lindsay Clancy was back in court today.
Her attorneys want a judge to dismiss the murder case against her,
saying it amounts to double jeopardy.
NPR's Bill Chappell with details.
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial ended in a mistrial two months ago after jurors deadlocked on whether
she's criminally responsible for killing her three young children.
All but one accepted the defense's claim that her actions were driven by postpartum psychosis.
Judge William Sullivan of Plymouth Superior Court now plans to rule on whether to dismiss
the case altogether on November 16th.
Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague says that in Massachusetts,
"I couldn't find a single case where there was a mistrial and then a motion to dismiss
was allowed on the grounds of double jeopardy."
The judge says that if he rules against dismissing the case, attorneys should be
ready to pick a new trial date, possibly next spring.
Bill Chappell, NPR News.
From Washington, this is NPR.
The National Transportation Safety Board has given an update on the business jet that crashed
into a neighborhood in Palm Beach, Florida yesterday.
All nine people onboard the Learjet, two flight crew and seven passengers were killed.
There were reports of an injured person as well on the ground.
LiveATC.net has air traffic control recordings from the plane
that began its flight in Austin, Texas and was flying east at 35,000 feet bound for the Bahamas.
The pilot is heard reporting ice on the jet requesting permission to climb 2,000 feet
and then quickly issuing a May Day in reporting the plane's rapid descent.
Recordings show the small aircraft heading to the ground like a missile and exploding in flames.
A new survey shows manufacturing in the United States is picking up steam,
but as NPR's Scott Horsley explains, the factory sector still faces some serious headwinds.
The survey shows factory orders, output and employment all grew last month,
a generally healthy sign for the manufacturing sector.
But Susan Spence, who conducts the survey for the Institute for Supply Management,
says two-thirds of factory managers had complaints
that tariffs, supply shortages or price hikes tied to the war with Iran
are preventing a bigger manufacturing boom.
"If we had the war over or resolved or super, super close to resolution,
then I feel like the floodgates would open."
Spence says sentiment among factory managers worsened in October for the third month in a row.
